hints: Focus on the number of gases produced, as carbonates and nitrates decompose in very different ways.
Recall that a Group 2 nitrate gives an oxide plus two gases, $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$, while a carbonate gives only $\text{CO}_2$.
Now compare cations for the same anion, remembering that the smaller, more polarising $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ion distorts the anion more and lowers thermal stability.
walkthrough:
**Use the number of gases to find the anion**

Think about what each type of compound makes when heated. This is your biggest clue.

Carbonate decomposition:
$$\text{MCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{MO} + \text{CO}_2$$
Only one gas is formed.

Nitrate decomposition:
$$2\text{M}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$
Two different gases are formed.

**Conclude Z must be a nitrate**

The question says Z produces two different gases. That matches only the nitrate reaction, not the carbonate reaction.
So we can rule out both carbonates and keep only the two nitrates.

**Use thermal stability to find the cation**

Thermal stability of Group 2 compounds increases down the group. A small cation with high charge density polarises and weakens the anion more, so it decomposes more easily.
$\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is much smaller than $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, so magnesium compounds are less thermally stable than barium compounds with the same anion.
Since Z has relatively low stability, Z must contain magnesium.

**Put both clues together**

Anion must be nitrate (two gases). Cation must be magnesium (low stability).
Therefore Z is magnesium nitrate.

options.A: Incorrect. Barium carbonate decomposes to $\text{BaO} + \text{CO}_2$, which is only one gas, not two. It is also very thermally stable because $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is large and weakly polarising.
options.B: Incorrect. Barium nitrate does give two gases ($\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$), so the anion is right, but the cation is wrong. Barium compounds have high thermal stability down the group, while Z is described as having relatively low stability.
options.C: Incorrect. Magnesium carbonate does have low thermal stability due to the small $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ion, but it decomposes to $\text{MgO} + \text{CO}_2$, which is only one gas. The two-gases clue points to a nitrate.
options.D: Correct. Magnesium nitrate decomposes as $2\text{Mg}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MgO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$, giving two different gases. Magnesium is at the top of Group 2, so its small, highly polarising $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ion gives it low thermal stability compared to other Group 2 nitrates.
